## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: As the first screen, it is plainly the check of whether I am the right person, and I take booking calls in our Munich central reservations office, so I can see why it is asked.
screens.why2: Reservations, hotel group, central reservations office and call centre are the everyday words of my job, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I work and how our group handles reservations, so I answer from fact, not a guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover every case for a gate question, and they do not overlap.
screens.why5: It keeps the segment of agents at German hotel groups with a central office or call centre, and nothing about any product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one question of 19 words with two short options, easy to hear once and answer, and the gate correctly has no escape.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking about my last week of booking calls is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand it at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether calls came in on my shifts this week, since that is my whole job.
screens.why4: Yes and No answer this stem cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: The founder counted calls that do not get answered, but this asks only whether a call came in, so the condition that made it a problem is gone and the meaning is wrong.
screens.why6: One short sentence, then 'Yes or no', is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: This gate asks about the circumstance every reservation agent is in, so everyone says Yes, No is left to nobody, and the founder's share can never be refuted, which is the card's bad example exactly.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered? Yes · No

screens.why1: A count after the yes at the gate is expected, but for me it only asks how many shifts I worked, since every shift in our central office has booking calls.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are exactly how we talk on the reservations floor, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know my own rota for the last week and that calls came in on each shift, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer, with no overlap and no zero, and I can't recall fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The founder's point was that not every call gets answered, and that has dropped out, so the screen now counts days with calls rather than days the problem happened.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and 'Say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold.
screens.why7: The measure, shape, order and escape all match the card, but the event is just a call arriving, which happens on every shift, so the count tracks days worked and almost every answer will land on the supporting side.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did a booking call ring out on your shift without anyone picking up? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Straight after asking how many days booking calls came in, it makes sense to ask which part of my shift I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: Rates on every channel, check-in rush and group requests are all everyday words in my trade, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I work in the central reservations office in Munich, not at a front desk, so 'handling guests' requests at the desk' and 'the check-in and check-out rush' are someone else's shift and I would be guessing about them.
screens.why4: Two of the five rows are front-desk work I never do, and 'booking emails and group requests' holds two tasks in one row, so I really only have three options that fit my office.
screens.why5: 'Picking up every booking call' keeps the founder's problem of calls going unanswered, and nothing about a product or the company's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options read as a list and one escape at the end, easy to hold on the phone.
screens.why7: The own row is there and not first, the escape is at the first ask, and there are enough other rows to refute it, but two rivals have drifted to front-desk work for a central reservations office (the card's named pitfall) and one row joins emails and group requests.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift in the reservations office. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping rates right on every channel · Answering booking emails · Handling group booking requests · Changing and cancelling existing bookings · Picking up every booking call · None of these

screens.why1: After asking which part of a shift I'd most like made easier, asking how answering calls actually went on my last shift is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "How did getting a booking call answered go" is clumsy; I'd say "how did answering the booking calls go", and I have to read it twice to see what is being asked.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last shift went with calls ringing out and callbacks, but the stem asks about one booking call, so I'd have to guess that it means the whole shift.
screens.why4: The five rungs are distinct and sound like how we talk about missed calls, but every one describes many calls, so none fits the single call the stem asks about; "answered or called back" also joins two outcomes in the first rung.
screens.why5: Nothing about any product or the founder's terms reaches me; rang out, called back and lost calls are my own words.
screens.why6: It is one question and five options a listener can hold, but the clumsy stem and the long first option with its "or" are a mouthful when heard once.
screens.why7: The scale has a working first rung, worsening shortfalls and an outright failure as the last rung, all on one measure (calls lost or recovered), and it carries one escape, but the stem's occasion (one call) doesn't match what the options measure (a shift's calls), which bends the card's rule that the options answer the exact question.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift in the reservations office. How did answering the booking calls go? -- Every call answered or called back within minutes · A few rang out, all called back that day · Some rang out, called back when there was time · Many rang out, few were called back · Calls that rang out were simply lost · Someone else took the calls
